claims.text: Carbon fiber–reinforced polymer composites at around 60% fiber volume fraction can have higher specific tensile strength than aluminum 7075 under equivalent load conditions.
Carbon fiber–reinforced polymer composites at around 60% fiber volume fraction can have higher specific stiffness than aluminum 7075 under equivalent load conditions.
The carbon fiber volume fraction can be varied from 40% to 70% while holding resin type, curing temperature, and pressure constant.
Consistent humidity and loading rates during room-temperature testing will improve reproducibility across samples.
The fiber–matrix interface bond facilitates load transfer between the polymer matrix and carbon fibers.
The fiber–matrix interface influences the overall mechanical performance of the composite.
A strong and uniform fiber–matrix interface promotes efficient transfer of load from the polymer matrix to the carbon fibers.
Efficient load transfer through the fiber–matrix interface enhances composite strength relative to density.
Efficient load transfer through the fiber–matrix interface enhances composite stiffness relative to density.
Composite specimens at approximately 60% fiber volume fraction will have higher tensile strength per unit mass than an aluminum 7075 control.
Composite specimens at approximately 60% fiber volume fraction will have higher stiffness per unit mass than an aluminum 7075 control.
Fiber volume fractions significantly above or below approximately 60% may reduce composite mechanical performance.
Performance losses at fiber volume fractions significantly above or below approximately 60% may prevent the composite from outperforming aluminum 7075.
Fiber grade, resin grade, fabrication method, and test protocol can alter composite microstructure and mechanical properties.
